title: Subways, Strikes, and Slowdowns: The Impacts of Public Transit on Traffic Congestion
research_question: How does the provision of public transit service affect traffic congestion on roadways in a large metropolitan area, and how large are the resulting congestion-relief benefits relative to the costs of operating and building transit systems?
data_description: The empirical analysis uses hourly traffic data from the California Department of Transportation's Performance Measurement System (PeMS), which collects vehicle counts and average speeds from embedded loop detectors on major divided freeways (average detector spacing of 0.6 miles). The unit of observation is the detector-by-hour. Key variables include average speed, average delay (minutes per mile relative to a 60 mph free-flow speed), hourly vehicle flows per lane, and share of time a detector is occupied. The sample covers all major Los Angeles County freeways during weekday peak periods (7-10 am and 2-8 pm), with a 28-day window on each side of October 14, 2003. Falsification samples include freeways in neighboring Orange and Ventura counties and Los Angeles freeways one year later (October-November 2004). Supplementary data on ridership, fares, wages, and travel parameters come from LACMTA, BLS, AAA, and Parry and Small (2009).
institutional_context: The setting is the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), which provides heavy rail, light rail, and bus service to roughly 10 million people across a 1,400 square mile area, carrying about 200,000 daily rail boardings and 1.1 million daily bus boardings in 2003. On October 14, 2003, MTA mechanics began a strike—triggered by a dispute over health-care fund contributions—on the first business day after a 60-day court-ordered injunction expired. Drivers, clerks, and supervisors honored the picket line, shutting down essentially the entire bus and rail system for 35 days until November 18, 2003, when service resumed gradually. A small number of contracted bus routes and Metrolink commuter rail continued but carried a negligible share of riders. Private automobiles account for over 98 percent of regional passenger miles, with congestion levels above the national urban average. The abrupt, exogenously timed cessation of transit service offers a sharp change in transit availability while roadway capacity remained constant.
